transcript: Correction: I grew sorghum last season, not maize. My farm is still in Kajuru, Kaduna. My priorities are soil fertility and lower inputs.
advice_text:
==============================================================================
CROP ROTATION ADVICE FOR YOUR FARM
Place: Kajuru, Kaduna (North West)
Weather data: NASA POWER 2001 to 2025. Soil: iSDAsoil.
Made on: 2026-11-15
==============================================================================

THIS IS ADVICE TO TALK ABOUT, NOT AN ORDER.
Please show it to your extension agent. They know your field, your market and
the local rules. This tool has not seen your field.
Do not buy or mix fertiliser or chemicals from this page. Ask your extension
agent for the amount for your own plot.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. YOUR LAND
- Soil acidity (pH): about 5.7. The soil map says it is most likely between
  5.5 and 5.9.
- The soil is sandy clay loam, both at the top and deeper down.
- Organic carbon in the top 20 cm: 6.4 g per kg. A soil test would tell you
  how this compares with good soil.
- The land slopes about 2 degrees at this spot (flat ground is 0).
- The soil acidity estimate is in the best range for: Cassava, Cowpea (beans),
  Groundnut (peanut), Maize, Millet, Rice, Sorghum (guinea corn), Soybean.
- The soil may be too acid for: Yam.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. RAIN AND THE GROWING SEASON
- In a normal year about 1,370 mm of rain falls.
- The rains usually start around 31 May and the growing season ends around 5
  Nov, roughly 165 days. This is a computer estimate from weather data.
- In about 1 year out of 4 the season is only 142 days or shorter.
- The weather source gave rain totals that look wrong for 2020, 2021, 2022. We
  left those years out. Please do not trust year-to-year rain details too
  much.
- The planting months in section 4 are what farmers in your zone report. They
  can differ from the computer estimate above. Trust what you and your
  neighbours know.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. WHAT YOU TOLD US
- Last season: Sorghum (guinea corn)
- You told us about one season, so we cannot see a pattern.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. YOUR CHOICES
Do not buy or mix fertiliser or chemicals from this page. Ask your extension
agent for the amount for your own plot.

CHOICE 1: KEEP WHAT YOU DO NOW
  CEREAL AFTER CEREAL
  What it is: You grow cereals such as maize, sorghum, millet or rice one
  season after another.
  Year by year:
    Year 1: Sorghum (guinea corn), usually planted Apr to Jul
    Year 2: Sorghum (guinea corn), usually planted Apr to Jul
    Year 3: Sorghum (guinea corn), usually planted Apr to Jul
    Year 4: Sorghum (guinea corn), usually planted Apr to Jul
  How the crops fit your land (out of 100): Sorghum (guinea corn) 70.
  What may help:
    - You need no new seed or market.
    - Sorghum and millet cope with less rain than maize.
  What to watch out for:
    - Striga, a parasitic weed, attacks maize, sorghum, rice and millet, so
      changing from one cereal to another is unlikely to reduce it.
    - Fall armyworm attacks maize, rice and sorghum.
    - Maize every season uses up soil nitrogen and organic matter. In one
      Nigerian trial, maize yields fell over the years.
    - Sorghum smut can stay in the soil for years, so grow sorghum on the same
      field only once in four years.
  Problems we found in this plan:
    - Years 1, 2, 3, 4: head smut lives in the soil for years, so grow sorghum
      on the same field only once in 4 years
  How it lines up with what matters to you:
    - Add organic matter and keep crop residue: this is the comparison point
    - Keep seed, fertiliser and labour needs low: this is the comparison point
  How sure we are: some evidence. Tested in: trials at Ibadan and Zaria and
  reviews across Africa.
  Ask: your extension agent about checking for Striga and armyworm on your
  field.

CHOICE 2: ANOTHER WAY TO ROTATE
  A LEGUME AND A CEREAL IN TURNS
  What it is: You grow a legume (cowpea, groundnut or soybean) one season and
  a cereal the next, in turns.
  Year by year:
    Year 1: Cowpea (beans), usually planted May to Aug
    Year 2: Millet, usually planted Apr to Jul
    Year 3: Cowpea (beans), usually planted May to Aug
    Year 4: Millet, usually planted Apr to Jul
  How the crops fit your land (out of 100): Cowpea (beans) 90, Millet 80.
  The tests above were done with other crops. For Millet the evidence is
  weaker or missing.
  What may help:
    - Across Africa, a cereal grown after a legume gave on average about 41%
      more grain than a cereal after a cereal, about 0.49 tonnes per hectare
      (about 200 kg per acre). Maize responded more than sorghum or millet,
      but that comparison is weak and the gain for sorghum and millet was not
      certain.
    - Legumes can put nitrogen into the soil. In the northern savanna soybean
      left about 56 to 95 kg of nitrogen per hectare (about 23 to 38 kg per
      acre), but only when its roots are counted and the stalks stay in the
      field. When the grain is taken away the balance is often negative.
    - On 12 farmers' fields in Kaduna that had Striga, maize after cowpea gave
      21% more grain than maize after maize. That trial used Striga-resistant
      maize and 100 kg of nitrogen per hectare (about 40 kg per acre), and the
      gain may be smaller where there is no Striga or less fertiliser.
    - Soybean and groundnut are the most sold of the crops compared (61% and
      57% of the harvest is sold, against 34% for sorghum and 33% for millet).
  What to watch out for:
    - In the drier Sahel zone the gains were smaller and not certain.
    - The gain gets smaller when you put on more nitrogen fertiliser.
    - In the South West and South East, trials found mixed gains after cowpea
      and soybean.
    - Legumes need good seed, and often phosphorus, drainage and deep enough
      soil. Check these on your field.
  How it lines up with what matters to you:
    - Add organic matter and keep crop residue: no clear benefit found
    - Keep seed, fertiliser and labour needs low: needs extra seed, inoculant
      or work
  How sure we are: some evidence. Tested in: farmers' fields in Kaduna, trials
  at Zaria and Ibadan, and reviews across Africa.
  Ask: your extension agent and a seed supplier about phosphorus, drainage and
  seed.

CHOICE 3: ANOTHER WAY TO ROTATE
  A LONGER ROTATION OF THREE OR FOUR SEASONS
  What it is: You follow a cereal with a legume, then a different cereal, then
  a different legume.
  Year by year:
    Year 1: Cowpea (beans), usually planted May to Aug
    Year 2: Millet, usually planted Apr to Jul
    Year 3: Soybean, usually planted May to Jul
    Year 4: Rice, usually planted Apr to Jul
  How the crops fit your land (out of 100): Cowpea (beans) 90, Millet 80, Rice
  90, Soybean 100.
  No test measured this exact pattern.
  What may help:
    - Each crop comes back less often, which helps against diseases that stay
      in the soil (for sorghum, one crop in four years on the same field;
      groundnut should not be repeated on the same field).
    - Your income and risk are spread over more crops.
    - A legume comes in two of every four seasons.
  What to watch out for:
    - It will not clear Striga seed, which can stay in the soil for 15 to 20
      years.
    - No Nigerian trial compares a long rotation with a short one.
    - More crops need more labour, seed and markets.
  How it lines up with what matters to you:
    - Add organic matter and keep crop residue: we do not know yet
    - Keep seed, fertiliser and labour needs low: the evidence says: highest
      complexity
  How sure we are: little evidence. Tested in: no trial of this exact pattern
  in Nigeria, only farmers' own reports from Kano and Kaduna.
  Ask: your extension agent about labour, seed and markets for the extra
  crops.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. CROPS THAT FIT YOUR LAND
The number is out of 100. A higher number means the crop fits your land and
climate better. It does not predict your harvest.
  Cassava: 100 (all checks fine)
  Groundnut (peanut): 100 (all checks fine)
  Soybean: 100 (all checks fine)
  Cowpea (beans): 90 (temperature a little too low)
  Maize: 90 (yearly rain a little too high)
  Rice: 90 (yearly rain a little too low)
  Millet: 80 (yearly rain a little too high; temperature a little too low)
  Sorghum (guinea corn): 70 (yearly rain too high for it)
  Yam: 57 (the soil may be too acid for it; the soil acidity estimate is
  uncertain; temperature a little too low)
The check on yearly rain is rough: the tables we use do not say if their rain
range is for a year or for the growing season.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. KEEPING SOIL AND WATER
These are things that keep soil and water. Each one comes from a study; ask
your extension agent which fit your field.
  - Keep the soil covered with residue or mulch
  - Cover about 70 to 75 percent of the soil surface, which needs 4 to 6
    tonnes per hectare (about 1.6 to 2.4 tonnes per acre) of mulch
  - Do not leave long bare fallow periods
  - A cover crop between rows cuts soil loss compared with sole maize
  - Reduced or no tillage keeps more soil moisture
  - A legume cover crop uses soil water while it grows and conserves it
    afterwards

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. WHAT WE DO NOT KNOW, AND WHAT TO CHECK
We do not have these things, so please check them yourself or with your agent:
  - Get a soil test. The soil numbers above are computer estimates for a 30 m
    square, not a measurement on your field.
  - We do not know your field size, drainage or flooding, whether you own or
    rent the land, your labour, your seed and fertiliser supply, or your
    market. Those decide a lot.
  - We do not know if Striga is on your field. Ask your agent to help you
    look.
  - Satellite pictures of green plants and soil moisture are not prepared for
    your area, so they were not used.
  - The soil acidity numbers are estimates and could be wrong for: Yam. A soil
    test will settle it.
  - In some years your season is shorter than a normal year, so ask which
    crops and varieties suit a short season.
  - More choices fit your area than we show: N10. Ask your agent.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. SMALL PRINT
Weather: NASA POWER (modelled). Soil: iSDAsoil (modelled, 30 m). Slope:
NASADEM (NASA). Crop needs: EcoCrop and FAO tables. Rotation evidence:
published Nigerian and African studies listed in the detailed file.
Units: 1 hectare is about 2.5 acres, and the figures per acre are worked out
from the ones per hectare. kg = kilograms, t = tonnes, mm = millimetres of
rain, g per kg = grams per kilogram. Kilograms of nitrogen or phosphorus are
the plant food in the fertiliser, not the weight of the bag: your agent can
tell you how many bags that is.
A longer report for your extension agent is available as a file.
This tool supports your judgment and your extension agent. It does not replace
them.
==============================================================================
